To further evaluate the production capacity of the engineered strain, fed-batch bioconversion of the best-performing strain was carried out. This study aimed to explore the limitations of resting cell bioconversion using a formaldehyde-fed batch process to enhance ethylene glycol titer and prolong bioconversion duration. Using 96 well plates without O control, we initiated the process with 10 mM 2 formaldehyde and 20 mM formate, feeding 5 mM formaldehyde every hour and 20 mM formate every three hours (Figure 35 A, D). The ethylene glycol concentration increased, reaching the first plateau around 5 hours. After 6 hours, it continued increasing, likely due to formate feeding, which provided extra NADH to drive the 50 reaction toward ethylene glycol production. After 9 hours, the ethylene glycol concentration reached 9.8 mM. Byproducts such as glycolate increased slowly while glycolaldehyde levels remained constant. Under completely anaerobic conditions in Hungate tubes, formate was primarily consumed initially when there was still some dissolved O in the buffer. We added 10 2 mM formaldehyde and 20 mM formate, feeding only 5 mM formaldehyde every hour (Figure 35 B, E). Unlike the deep-well plates, the ethylene glycol titer in Hungate tubes kept increasing without any plateau, reaching 18 mM at 9 hours. Byproducts, glycolaldehyde, and glycolate remained at low concentrations, increasing slightly. Notably, formate consumption was minimal initially but increased by the end of bioconversion, possibly due to air introduction during feeding, which supported NADH production necessary for the reaction. Formaldehyde consumption continued until 8 hours, indicating that resting cells remained active for at least this duration.
